title: Doubling the Zanzibar and the Roxy; Sleepy drops his trumpet
summary: The band worked the Roxy and the Zanzibar in the same day, and a sleepy trumpet player dropped his horn during Bill Robinson's soft shoe.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: would be in front of the band, we'd play the music and he would be singing and I'd read my music, play with the section and listen to him perform the projection of the melody, the way he'd perform and we'd perform with Velma Middleton, and stayed there, we worked there for a space of about three weeks, after three weeks we were engaged to also play at the Roxy Theater and the following two weeks or was it three weeks, I'm not sure, it was the hardest work I had ever done up to that point. I did some hard work, too, while I was in Louie, and we would open up in the afternoon, we'd play the first show at the Roxy and then going to the second show. Then after the second show, we'd have to report back to the Zanzibar to play the first show at the Zanzibar. So in between the rest of the night we alternated between the two shows. And it was quite hard to go back and forth, each performance we had to change clothes and come back.

The Roxy Theater was right next to the Taft Hotel on, what is that, 53rd -- I think it's torn down now. But that whole show from the Zanzibar would go, we'd be at the Roxy, including Bill Robinson he was doing his solo, doing his soft shoe with his

with his steps, "Big Sleepy," Thomas Grider, one of the trumpet players he was always sleeping, would sleep anywhere and during the soft shoe where nothing but piano music was -- drums were playing rushes on there, snare drums, Sleepy fell asleep and he dropped his horn all the way down to the main floor. The band was elevated. What a crash that made with the trumpet and Bill Robinson was all flustered and you can imagine how Bill Robinson felt.
